summary: The X3 30e xDrive is the only plug-in hybrid in BMW Australia's G45 X3 range, pairing a 2.0-litre turbo petrol with a 19.7kWh usable battery for 220kW/450Nm and an 86km WLTP electric range (BMW quotes a 81-90km band) — roughly double the previous X3 PHEV and enough for most Australian buyers to commute on electricity alone. Reviewers rate the ride and the EV-mode refinement highly, and several nominate the 30e as the pick of the X3 range, but they are consistent about the trade-offs: the battery costs 110 litres of boot space, the brake pedal loses the feel of the petrol cars, and the engine audibly strains once the charge is gone. At $107,700 before on-roads for the MY26 car it sits well above both LCT thresholds, and with the FBT exemption for plug-in hybrids gone since April 2025 the case rests entirely on charging at home every night.
pros: 86km WLTP electric range (BMW's band is 81-90km) from a 19.7kWh usable battery — roughly double the 41km of the previous X3 xDrive30e — with reviewers reporting 70-80km in real Australian conditions, so a typical 30-45km commute runs on electricity alone
11kW three-phase AC charging is standard (up from 7.4kW on the pre-update car), giving a full charge in about 2 hours 15 minutes rather than an overnight-only proposition
2000kg braked towing and 220kW/450Nm for a 6.2-second 0-100km/h means the plug-in doesn't give away capability to the 20 xDrive petrol it costs more than

38g/km combined CO2 puts it comfortably under Victoria's 120g/km green passenger car threshold, so it attracts the $8.40-per-$200 duty rate instead of the $14.00-per-$200 tier a $100,000-plus petrol X3 pays — worth roughly $3,000 at this price

Five years/unlimited kilometres vehicle warranty with a separate six-year/100,000km high-voltage battery warranty, and M Sport package, panoramic roof and adaptive LED headlights are standard rather than optional
cons: The battery sits under the boot floor and costs 110 litres: 460L seats-up versus 570L in the 20 xDrive and M50, and 1600L versus 1700L folded — the Mercedes GLC 350e and Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid also carry more claimed electric range

The 1.6L/100km label figure is meaningless once the battery is flat: ADAC's WLTP battery-empty figure is 7.7L/100km and its own Ecotest averaged 8.1L/100km in hybrid mode, and BMW Blog recorded around 14L/100km driving a depleted 30e in Sport mode, so a buyer without home charging is running a 2065kg petrol SUV

PHEVs lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, and at $107,700 the X3 30e is above both the $80,809 ordinary and $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT thresholds and far above the $75,000 FBT cap — the concessions that made this car a novated-lease case are gone
AC-only charging at 11kW with no DC fast-charge capability, where the Mercedes GLC 350e accepts up to 60kW, and no vehicle-to-load or vehicle-to-home output

Multiple reviewers flag a soft, indistinct brake pedal from the regenerative blending — carsales called it 'squashy' versus the petrol variants — and CarExpert notes the engine 'sounds and feels like it has to work hard' climbing hills on a low battery
